entries.literal: Han sent Guozi libationer Tian Min as envoy to Chu, passing through Jingnan by courtesy; Conghui asked Min about the strength and weakness of the central state, believing that after the Khitans troops and provisions were exhausted, intending to mock Min; Min replied: "Du Chongwei surrendered all Jin arms and armor to the invaders; the invaders placed them at Zhen Prefecture and have never brought them north, while the Jin troops are all in Han's possession."

entries.zh: 從誨不悅。
entries.en: Conghui was displeased.
entries.literal: Conghui was displeased.

entries.zh: 敏以印本《五經》遺從誨，從誨謝曰：「予之所識，不過《孝經》十八章爾。」
entries.en: Min presented printed copies of the Five Classics. Conghui declined, saying, "All I know are the eighteen chapters of the Classic of Filial Piety."
entries.literal: Min presented Conghui with printed copies of the Five Classics; Conghui declined and said: "What I know is no more than the eighteen chapters of the Classic of Filial Piety."

entries.zh: 敏曰：「至德要道，於此足矣。」
entries.en: Min said, "The utmost virtue and the essential Way are fully contained in that."
entries.literal: Min said: "The utmost virtue and essential Way are fully contained in that."

entries.zh: 敏因誦《諸侯章》曰：「在上不驕，高而不危，制節謹度，滿而不溢。」
entries.en: Min then recited the chapter on feudal lords: "Not arrogant when above others, lofty yet not endangered, restraining oneself and observing measure, full yet not overflowing."
entries.literal: Min then recited the chapter on feudal lords: "Not arrogant when above others, lofty yet not endangered, restraining oneself and observing measure, full yet not overflowing."

entries.zh: 從誨以為譏己，即以大卮罰敏。
entries.en: Conghui took this as a personal rebuke and immediately forced Min to drink a huge cup of wine as punishment.
entries.literal: Conghui took it as a satire on himself and at once punished Min with a large cup of wine.

entries.zh: 保融字德長。
entries.en: Baorong, whose courtesy name was Dechang.
entries.literal: Baorong, courtesy name Dechang.

entries.zh: 從誨時，為節度副使，兼峽州刺史。
entries.en: Under Conghui he served as deputy military governor and concurrently as prefect of Xia Prefecture.
entries.literal: During Conghui's time he was deputy military governor and concurrently prefect of Xia Prefecture.

entries.zh: 從誨卒，拜節度使。
entries.en: When Conghui died he was appointed military governor.
entries.literal: When Conghui died he was appointed military governor.

entries.zh: 廣順元年，封渤海郡王。
entries.en: In the first year of Guangshun he was enfeoffed as Prince of Bohai.
entries.literal: In the first year of Guangshun he was enfeoffed as Prince of Bohai commandery.

entries.zh: 顯德元年，進封南平王。
entries.en: In the first year of Xiande he was promoted to Prince of Nanping.
entries.literal: In the first year of Xiande he was advanced to Prince of Nanping.

entries.zh: 世宗征淮，保融遣指揮使魏璘率兵三千，出夏口以為應。
entries.en: When Emperor Shizong campaigned on the Huai, Baorong sent the commander Wei Lin with three thousand men from Xiakou in support.
entries.literal: When Emperor Shizong campaigned in Huai, Baorong sent the commander Wei Lin leading three thousand troops out from Xiakou in support.

entries.zh: 又遣客將劉扶奉箋南唐，勸其內附。
entries.en: He also sent the guest officer Liu Fu with a memorial to Southern Tang urging submission to the central court.
entries.literal: He also sent the guest officer Liu Fu with a memorial to Southern Tang urging it to submit inward.

entries.zh: 李景稱臣，世宗得保融所與箋，大喜，賜以絹百匹。
entries.en: When Li Jing submitted, Shizong obtained Baorong's memorial and was delighted, rewarding him with a hundred bolts of silk.
entries.literal: When Li Jing submitted as a minister, Shizong obtained the memorial Baorong had sent him and was greatly pleased, bestowing a hundred bolts of silk.

entries.zh: 荊南自後唐以來，常數歲一貢京師，而中間兩絕。
entries.en: Since Later Tang, Jingnan had usually sent tribute to the capital every few years, though twice it had broken off entirely.
entries.literal: Since Later Tang, Jingnan had usually sent tribute to the capital every few years, but twice interrupted the practice.

entries.zh: 及世宗時，無歲不貢矣。
entries.en: Under Shizong it sent tribute every year without fail.
entries.literal: By Shizong's time there was no year without tribute.

entries.zh: 保融以謂器械金帛，皆土地常產，不足以效誠節，乃遣其弟保紳來朝，世宗益嘉之。
entries.en: Baorong felt that arms, armor, gold, and silk were merely ordinary local products and insufficient proof of loyalty, so he sent his younger brother Baoshen to court in person. Shizong was still more pleased.
entries.literal: Baorong held that weapons, armor, gold, and silk were all ordinary products of the land and insufficient to show sincerity and loyalty; he therefore sent his younger brother Baoshen to court, and Shizong was all the more pleased.

entries.zh: 繼沖字成和。
entries.en: Jichong, whose courtesy name was Chenghe.
entries.literal: Jichong, courtesy name Chenghe.

entries.zh: 保勖卒，拜節度使。
entries.en: When Baoxun died he was appointed military governor.
entries.literal: When Baoxun died he was appointed military governor.

entries.zh: 湖南周行逢卒，子保權立，其將張文表作亂，建隆四年，太祖命慕容延釗等討之。
entries.en: When Zhou Xingfeng of Hunan died, his son Baoquan succeeded him, but his general Zhang Wenbiao rebelled. In the fourth year of Jianlong the Founding Emperor ordered Murong Yanzhao and others to suppress the revolt.
entries.literal: Zhou Xingfeng of Hunan died; his son Baoquan succeeded; his general Zhang Wenbiao rebelled; in the fourth year of Jianlong the Founding Emperor ordered Murong Yanzhao and others to campaign against him.

entries.zh: 延釗假道荊南，約以兵過城外。
entries.en: Yanzhao sought passage through Jingnan on the understanding that his army would march outside the city walls.
entries.literal: Yanzhao asked passage through Jingnan, agreeing that his troops would pass outside the city walls.

entries.zh: 繼沖大將李景威曰：「兵尚權譎，城外之約，不可信也。
entries.en: Jichong's chief general Li Jingwei said, "War favors stratagem and deceit. An agreement to pass outside the walls cannot be trusted.
entries.literal: Jichong's great general Li Jingwei said: "Warfare values stratagem and deceit; an agreement to pass outside the walls cannot be trusted.

entries.zh: 宜嚴兵以待之。」
entries.en: We should mobilize our forces and stand ready."
entries.literal: We should array strict troops to await them."

entries.zh: 判官孫光憲叱之曰：「汝峽江一民爾，安識成敗！
entries.en: The administrative aide Sun Guangxian rebuked him: "You are nothing but a commoner of the gorges—what do you know of success or failure!
entries.literal: The administrative aide Sun Guangxian rebuked him and said: "You are but a commoner of the Gorges and rivers—how would you know success or failure!

entries.zh: 且中國自周世宗時，已有混一天下之志，況聖宋受命，真主出邪！
entries.en: The central state has sought to unite the realm ever since Emperor Shizong of Zhou. How much more now that sacred Song has received the Mandate and the true ruler has appeared!
entries.literal: Moreover the central state, from the time of Emperor Shizong of Zhou, already had the will to unite the realm; how much more now that sacred Song has received the Mandate and the true ruler has appeared!

entries.zh: 王師豈易當也！」
entries.en: Imperial troops are not to be resisted lightly!"
entries.literal: How easily could imperial troops be resisted!"

entries.zh: 因勸繼沖去斥候，封府庫以待，繼沖以為然。
entries.en: He urged Jichong to withdraw the scouts, seal the treasury, and wait peacefully. Jichong agreed.
entries.literal: He thereupon urged Jichong to remove scouts, seal the treasury and storehouses, and wait; Jichong thought it right.

entries.zh: 景威出而嘆曰：「吾言不用，大事去矣，何用生為！」
entries.en: Jingwei left and sighed, "My counsel was ignored. The cause is lost. What point is there in going on!"
entries.literal: Jingwei went out and sighed: "My words are not used; the great affair is lost—what use is there in living!"

entries.zh: 因扼吭而死。
entries.en: He then strangled himself.
entries.literal: He thereupon seized his throat and died.

entries.zh: 延釗軍至，繼沖出逆於郊，而前鋒遽入其城。
entries.en: When Yanzhao's army arrived, Jichong went out to greet it in the suburbs, but the vanguard suddenly entered the city.
entries.literal: When Yanzhao's army arrived, Jichong went out to meet it in the suburbs, but the vanguard suddenly entered his city.

entries.zh: 繼沖亟歸，見旌旗甲馬，布列衢巷，大懼，即詣延釗納牌印，太祖優詔復命繼沖為節度使。
entries.en: Jichong rushed back to find banners, armor, and horses filling every street. Terrified, he went at once to Yanzhao and surrendered his command tally and seal. The Founding Emperor graciously reappointed him military governor.
entries.literal: Jichong hurried back, saw banners, flags, armor, and horses arrayed along the streets and lanes, was greatly afraid, and at once went to Yanzhao to surrender his command tally and seal; the Founding Emperor with a gracious edict again appointed Jichong military governor.

entries.zh: 初，季興之鎮，梁以兵五千為牙兵，衣食皆給於梁。
entries.en: When Jixing first took office, Liang provided five thousand guard troops whose food and clothing were supplied by the Liang court.
entries.literal: At first, when Jixing took the post, Liang supplied five thousand troops as his guard army, and their food and clothing were all provided by Liang.

entries.zh: 至明宗時，歲給以鹽萬三千石，後不復給。
entries.en: Under Mingzong the court granted thirteen thousand piculs of salt annually, but later stopped.
entries.literal: By Mingzong's time thirteen thousand piculs of salt were given yearly; later this was no longer supplied.

entries.zh: 及世宗平淮，故命泰州給之。
entries.en: After Shizong pacified the Huai region, he ordered Taizhou to resume the grant.
entries.literal: When Shizong pacified Huai, he therefore ordered Taizhou to supply it.

entries.zh: 劉旻，漢高祖母弟也。
entries.en: Liu Min was the full younger brother of Later Han's founding emperor.
entries.literal: Liu Min was the uterine younger brother of Emperor Gaozu of Han.

entries.zh: 初名崇，為人美須髯，目重瞳子。
entries.en: Born Chong, he was strikingly handsome, with a fine beard and mustache and double pupils.
entries.literal: His original name was Chong; he was a man of handsome beard and mustache, with double pupils in his eyes.

entries.zh: 少無賴，嗜酒好博，嘗黥為卒。
entries.en: As a young man he was unruly and dissolute, given to drink and dice, and at one point was branded and pressed into the ranks.
entries.literal: In his youth he was a scoundrel, addicted to wine and fond of gambling, and was once tattooed and made a common soldier.

entries.zh: 高祖事晉為河東節度使，以旻為都指揮使。
entries.en: While Gaozu was still in Jin's service as governor of Hedong, he made Min his chief commander.
entries.literal: When Gaozu served Jin as military governor of Hedong, he appointed Min commander-in-chief.

entries.zh: 高祖即帝位，以為太原尹、北京留守、同中書門下平章事。
entries.en: After Gaozu took the throne, Min was appointed prefect of Taiyuan, defender of the northern capital, and concurrent Grand Councillor.
entries.literal: When Gaozu ascended the throne, Min was made governor of Taiyuan, garrison commander of the Northern Capital, and Palace Attendant with joint authority as Grand Councillor.

entries.zh: 隱帝時，累加中書令。
entries.en: During the reign of the youthful Yin Emperor, he was promoted repeatedly until he held the post of Grand Secretary.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Yin, he was repeatedly promoted until he reached Grand Secretary.

entries.zh: 繼恩本姓薛氏，父釗為卒，旻以女妻之，生繼恩。
entries.en: Jien was born Xue; his father Zhao was a common soldier whom Min married to a daughter—thus Jien.
entries.literal: Jien was originally surnamed Xue; his father Zhao was a soldier; Min gave him his daughter in marriage and Jien was born.

entries.zh: 漢高祖以釗婿也，除其軍籍，置之門下。
entries.en: Gaozu, as Zhao was family, struck him from the rolls and kept him at court.
entries.literal: Gaozu of Han, because Zhao was his son-in-law, removed him from the military rolls and kept him at court.

entries.zh: 釗無材能，高祖衣食之而無所用。
entries.en: Zhao had no ability; Gaozu clothed and fed him but never employed him.
entries.literal: Zhao had no talent; Gaozu fed and clothed him but found no use for him.

entries.zh: 妻以旻女常居中，釗罕得見，釗常怏怏，因醉拔佩刀刺之，傷而不死，釗即自裁。
entries.en: Min's daughter kept to the inner quarters; Zhao seldom saw her, grew bitter, and once, drunk, stabbed her—she lived—and then killed himself.
entries.literal: His wife, Min's daughter, always stayed in the inner quarters; Zhao rarely saw her; Zhao was often discontent; once drunk he drew his sword and stabbed her; she was wounded but did not die; Zhao then killed himself.

entries.zh: 旻女後適何氏，生子繼元，而何氏及旻女皆卒。
entries.en: She later wed a He and bore Jiyuan; both she and the He clan died.
entries.literal: Min's daughter later married the He family and bore Jiyuan; both the He family and Min's daughter died.

entries.zh: 旻以其子承鈞無子，乃以二子命承鈞養為子。
entries.en: As Chengjun had no heir, Min had both boys adopted as his sons.
entries.literal: Because his son Chengjun had no sons, Min ordered the two boys adopted as Chengjun's sons.

entries.zh: 承鈞立，以繼恩為太原尹。
entries.en: On his accession Chengjun made Jien prefect of Taiyuan.
entries.literal: When Chengjun reigned he made Jien governor of Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 承鈞嘗謂郭無為曰：「繼恩純孝，然非濟世之才，恐不能了我家事。」
entries.en: Chengjun once told Guo Youwei, "Jien is dutiful but no statesman—I doubt he can settle our house's affairs."
entries.literal: Chengjun once told Guo Youwei: "Jien is purely filial, yet lacks talent to save the age—I fear he cannot finish my family's affairs."

entries.zh: 無為不對。
entries.en: Youwei said nothing.
entries.literal: Youwei did not answer.

entries.zh: 承鈞病臥勤政閣，召無為，執手以後事付之。
entries.en: Dying in the Diligence Pavilion, he summoned Youwei, clasped his hand, and entrusted the aftermath.
entries.literal: Chengjun lay ill in the Diligence-in-Government Pavilion, summoned Youwei, took his hand and entrusted him with later affairs.

entries.zh: 承鈞，旻次子也。
entries.en: Chengjun was Min's second son.
entries.literal: Chengjun was Min's second son.

entries.zh: 少頗好學，工書。
entries.en: He had been studious as a youth and wrote a fine hand.
entries.literal: In youth he was quite studious and skilled at calligraphy.

entries.zh: 旻卒，承鈞遣人奉表契丹，自稱男。
entries.en: On Min's death he sent Khitan a petition calling himself the emperor's "boy."
entries.literal: When Min died, Chengjun sent a memorial to Khitan styling himself "your male child."

entries.zh: 述律答之以詔，呼承鈞為兒，許其嗣位。
entries.en: Shulü replied by edict, hailed him as "son," and confirmed his throne.
entries.literal: Shulü answered with an edict, addressing Chengjun as "son," and granted his succession.

entries.zh: 初，旻常謂張元徽等曰：「吾以高祖之業，赟之冤，義不為郭公屈爾，期與公等勉力以復家國之仇。
entries.en: Min had told Yuanhui and others, "Gaozu's realm and Yun's blood forbid me to bend to Guo—we must regain our patrimony.
entries.literal: Formerly Min often told Zhang Yuanhui and others: "On account of Gaozu's enterprise and Yun's grievance, by right I cannot bow to Lord Guo; let us strive together to avenge our house and state.

entries.zh: 至於稱帝一方，豈獲已也，顧我是何天子，爾亦是何節度使？」
entries.en: Proclaiming myself emperor in one corner—was that my wish? Think what Son of Heaven I am, and what sort of governors you are!"
entries.literal: As for proclaiming myself emperor on one side, how could that be helped? Only consider what sort of Son of Heaven I am, and what sort of military governors you are?"

entries.zh: 故其僭號仍稱乾祐，不改元，不立宗廟，四時之祭，用家人禮。
entries.en: So his throne still bore the era Qianyou; no new reign title; no imperial temple; sacrifices followed family rites.
entries.literal: Therefore his usurped title still used Qianyou; he did not change the era name; he did not establish an ancestral temple; the seasonal sacrifices used household ritual.

entries.zh: 承鈞既立，始赦境內，改乾祐十年曰天會元年，立七廟於顯聖宮。
entries.en: Chengjun then declared amnesty, renamed Qianyou 10 as Tianhui 1, and raised seven shrines at Xiansheng Palace.
entries.literal: Once Chengjun reigned he first amnestied the realm, changed the tenth year of Qianyou to the first year of Tianhui, and erected seven temples at Xiansheng Palace.

entries.zh: 隱帝少，政在大臣，周太祖為樞密使，新討三叛，立大功，而與旻素有隙，旻頗不自安，謂判官鄭珙曰：「主上幼弱，政在權臣，而吾與郭公不葉，時事如何？」
entries.en: Yin was still a child, so state affairs were in the hands of the senior ministers. Guo Wei, lately appointed chief of the privy council, had just crushed the three major rebellions and won towering credit—yet he and Min had old grievances. Min grew increasingly uneasy and asked his staff officer Zheng Gong, "The Son of Heaven is young, and power sits with the men at court. Guo and I have never been on good terms—how do you read the situation?"
entries.literal: The emperor was young and power lay with the ministers. Zhou Taizu was Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs; he had just suppressed the Three Rebellions and won great merit, yet he and Min had long been at odds. Min felt quite ill at ease. He said to his aide Zheng Qing: "The sovereign is young and weak, and government rests with powerful ministers. Guo and I do not get on—what is to become of things?"

entries.zh: 珙曰：「漢政將亂矣！
entries.en: Gong replied, "The Han regime is heading for chaos!
entries.literal: Qing said: "The rule of Han is about to fall into chaos!

entries.zh: 晉陽兵雄天下，而地形險固，十州征賦足以自給。
entries.en: Jinyang commands the finest soldiers in the realm, and its mountains make it a natural fortress. Taxes from ten prefectures would be enough to keep you supplied.
entries.literal: The troops of Jinyang are the strongest under Heaven, and the terrain there is precipitous and secure; the revenues of ten prefectures are enough to sustain you on your own.

entries.zh: 公為宗室，不以此時為計，後必為人所制。」
entries.en: You are a kinsman of the house—if you fail to act now, others will certainly hem you in later."
entries.literal: You are of the imperial clan; if you do not take thought for yourself at this moment, you will later be controlled by others."

entries.zh: 旻曰：「子言，乃吾意也。」
entries.en: Min said, "That is precisely what I mean."
entries.literal: Min said: "Your words are exactly my own thought."

entries.zh: 乃罷上供征賦，收豪傑，籍丁民以益兵。
entries.en: He stopped sending tribute levies up to the capital, recruited bold spirits, and registered civilian males to swell his army.
entries.literal: He then stopped forwarding tax levies to the central court, gathered bold spirits, and registered male commoners to increase his troops.

entries.zh: 三年，周太祖起魏，隱帝遇弒，旻乃謀舉兵。
entries.en: In the third year Guo Wei rebelled in Wei; the young emperor was assassinated; Min now planned to take the field.
entries.literal: In the third year, Zhou Taizu rose in Wei; Emperor Yin was murdered; Min then plotted to raise troops.

entries.zh: 周太祖之自魏入也，反狀已白，而漢大臣不即推尊之，故未敢即立，乃白漢太后，立旻子赟為漢嗣，遣宰相馮道迎赟於徐州。
entries.en: When Guo marched out of Wei toward Luoyang, his treason was plain, but the Han court still would not proclaim him emperor, so he hesitated to take the throne outright. He had the empress dowager name Yun, Min's son, as heir and sent Feng Dao to fetch him from Xuzhou.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu marched from Wei toward the capital, his rebellion was already exposed, yet the Han ministers did not immediately acclaim him, so he did not dare to take the throne at once. He informed the Han empress dowager, installed Min's son Yun as heir to Han, and sent Grand Councillor Feng Dao to welcome Yun from Xuzhou.

entries.zh: 當是時，人皆知太祖之非實意也，旻獨喜曰：「吾兒為帝矣，何患！」
entries.en: All who watched knew Guo's pledge was hollow, yet Min alone rejoiced: "My son is emperor—what danger remains?"
entries.literal: At that time everyone knew the Taizu had no genuine intention, but Min alone rejoiced and said: "My son has become emperor—what is there to fear!"

entries.zh: 乃罷兵，遣人至京師。
entries.en: He stood down his army and sent envoys to the capital.
entries.literal: He then disbanded his troops and sent someone to the capital.

entries.zh: 周太祖少賤，黥其頸上為飛雀，世謂之郭雀兒。
entries.en: Guo Wei had begun life in the lowest ranks; a tattoo of a flying sparrow on his neck earned him the nickname Sparrow Guo.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu had been low-born in his youth; he was tattooed on the neck with a flying sparrow, and the world called him Guo the Sparrow.

entries.zh: 太祖見旻使者，具道所以立赟之意，因自指其頸以示使者曰：「自古豈有雕青天子？
entries.en: Receiving Min's messenger, he laid out at length why Yun should reign and, tapping his tattooed neck, asked, "When in history has a Son of Heaven borne a convict's mark?
entries.literal: The Taizu received Min's envoy, fully explained his reasons for enthroning Yun, and, pointing to his own neck, showed the envoy and said: "Since antiquity has there ever been a tattooed Son of Heaven?

entries.zh: 幸公無以我為疑。」
entries.en: I beg you not to doubt me for this."
entries.literal: May you, sir, not doubt me on that account."

entries.zh: 旻喜，益信以為然。
entries.en: Min was overjoyed and believed him all the more.
entries.literal: Min was delighted and believed it all the more firmly.

entries.zh: 太原少尹李驤曰：「郭公舉兵犯順，其勢不能為漢臣，必不為劉氏立後。」
entries.en: Li Xiang, deputy governor of Taiyuan, warned, "Guo has taken up arms against his sovereign; he cannot remain Han's minister and will never install a Liu heir."
entries.literal: Li Xiang, vice-prefect of Taiyuan, said: "Lord Guo has raised troops in violation of the throne; in his position he cannot remain a subject of Han and will certainly not establish a successor for the Liu house."

entries.zh: 因勸旻以兵下太行，控孟津以俟變，庶幾赟得立，赟立而罷兵可也。
entries.en: He urged Min to march through the Taihang passes, hold Meng Ford, and wait on events—perhaps Yun could still be seated; once Yun reigned, they could disband.
entries.literal: He therefore urged Min to lead troops down the Taihang range, seize Meng Ford to await developments, so that perhaps Yun might be enthroned; once Yun was enthroned, standing down the army would be possible.

entries.zh: 旻大罵曰：「驤腐儒，欲離間我父子！」
entries.en: Min roared, "You pedant—trying to set my son and me at odds!"
entries.literal: Min cursed loudly: "Xiang, you rotten Confucian—trying to drive a wedge between father and son!"

entries.zh: 命左右牽出斬之。
entries.en: He had attendants haul Xiang out and behead him.
entries.literal: He ordered his attendants to drag him out and execute him.

entries.zh: 驤臨刑嘆曰：「吾為愚人畫計，死誠宜矣！
entries.en: On the scaffold Xiang sighed, "I schemed for a fool—death is only fair.
entries.literal: At the block Xiang sighed and said: "I drew up plans for a fool—death is indeed fitting!

entries.zh: 然吾妻病，不可獨存，願與之俱死。」
entries.en: But my wife is ill and cannot survive alone; let us die together."
entries.literal: Yet my wife is ill; she cannot live on alone; I ask to die together with her."

entries.zh: 旻聞之，即並戮其妻於市，以其事白漢，以明無他。
entries.en: Hearing this, Min had Xiang's sick wife killed in the marketplace too, then wrote the court to prove his loyalty.
entries.literal: When Min heard this, he immediately had his wife executed in the market as well, reported the matter to Han to show he had no other intent.

entries.zh: 已而周太祖果代漢，降封赟湘陰公。
entries.en: Soon Guo replaced the Han dynasty and reduced Yun to Duke of Xiangyin.
entries.literal: Before long Zhou Taizu did indeed supplant Han and demoted Yun to Duke of Xiangyin.

entries.zh: 旻遣牙將李鋋奉書周太祖，求赟歸太原，而赟已死。
entries.en: Min sent an aide, Li Qian, petitioning for Yun's return to Taiyuan—but Yun was already dead.
entries.literal: Min sent his military tooth Li Qian with a letter to Zhou Taizu asking that Yun be returned to Taiyuan, but Yun was already dead.

entries.zh: 旻慟哭，為李驤立祠，歲時祠之。
entries.en: Min mourned bitterly, raised a shrine to Li Xiang, and sacrificed to him each year.
entries.literal: Min wept bitterly, built a shrine to Li Xiang, and offered sacrifice to him at the seasons.

entries.zh: 周太祖崩，旻聞之喜，遣使乞兵於契丹。
entries.en: When Guo Wei died Min rejoiced and asked the Khitans for troops.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu died; when Min heard it he rejoiced and sent envoys begging troops from Khitan.

entries.zh: 契丹遣楊袞將鐵馬萬騎及奚諸部兵五六萬人號稱十萬以助旻。
entries.en: Khitan sent Yang Gun with ten thousand armored horse and fifty or sixty thousand Xi and allied riders—nominally a hundred thousand—to reinforce him.
entries.literal: The Khitans sent Yang Gun leading ten thousand iron cavalry and fifty or sixty thousand troops of the Xi and other tribes, claiming one hundred thousand, to aid Min.

entries.zh: 旻以張元徽為先鋒，自將騎兵三萬攻潞州。
entries.en: He put Zhang Yuanhui in the van and led thirty thousand cavalry against Luzhou himself.
entries.literal: Min made Zhang Yuanhui vanguard and personally led thirty thousand horsemen to attack Luzhou.

entries.zh: 潞州李筠遣穆令鈞以步騎三千拒元徽於太平驛，元徽擊敗之，益圍潞州。
entries.en: Luzhou's Li Yun sent Mu Lingjun with three thousand mixed troops to meet Yuanhui at Taiping Post; Yuanhui smashed them and tightened the encirclement.
entries.literal: Li Yun of Luzhou sent Mu Lingjun with three thousand foot and horse to oppose Yuanhui at Taiping Station; Yuanhui routed him and pressed the siege of Luzhou tighter.

entries.zh: 承鈞由此益重儒者，以抱腹山人郭無為參議國政。
entries.en: Thereafter he prized scholars and installed the mountain man Guo Wuwei in counsel.
entries.literal: From this Chengjun valued scholars all the more and made the recluse Guo Youwei a participant in state affairs.

entries.zh: 無為，棣州人，方顙鳥喙，好學多聞，善談辯。
entries.en: A Di Prefecture man with high brow and hooked nose, widely read and silver-tongued.
entries.literal: Youwei was from Di Prefecture, with a broad forehead and beaklike nose, fond of study and widely informed, skilled at disputation.

entries.zh: 嘗衣褐為道士，居武當山。
entries.en: He had lived as a Daoist in brown on Wudang.
entries.literal: He had worn brown robes as a Daoist priest on Mount Wudang.

entries.zh: 周太祖討李守貞於河中，無為詣軍門上謁，詢以當世之務，太祖奇之。
entries.en: During Guo's siege of Li Shouzhen at Hezhong, Youwei appeared at camp and debated policy; Guo was impressed.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu besieged Li Shouzhen at Hezhong, Youwei came to the camp gate and was questioned on current affairs; the Taizu thought him remarkable.

entries.zh: 或謂太祖曰：「公為漢大臣，握重兵居外，而延縱橫之士，非所以防微慮遠之道也。」
entries.en: An aide warned, "A Han minister with armies abroad who hosts roaming strategists invites suspicion."
entries.literal: Someone told the Taizu: "You are a Han minister holding great armies abroad while entertaining roaming strategists—not the way to guard against small beginnings and plan far ahead."

entries.zh: 由是太祖不納。
entries.en: Guo declined him.
entries.literal: The Taizu therefore did not take him in.

entries.zh: 無為去，隱抱腹山。
entries.en: Youwei retired to Mount Baofu.
entries.literal: Youwei left and hid on Mount Baofu.

entries.zh: 承鈞內樞密使段常識之，薦其材，承鈞以諫議大夫召之，遂以為相。
entries.en: Duan Chang of the privy council praised him; Chengjun made him Remonstrance Officer, then chancellor.
entries.literal: Interior Commissioner Duan Chang knew him and recommended his talent; Chengjun summoned him as Remonstrance Officer and then made him chancellor.

entries.zh: 五年，宿衛殿直行首王隱、劉紹、趙鸞等謀作亂，事覺被誅，其詞連段常，乃罷常樞密為汾州刺史，縊殺之。
entries.en: Fifth year: guards Wang Yin, Liu Shao, Zhao Luan plotted treason, were killed, and implicated Chang—demoted to Fen prefect and strangled.
entries.literal: In the fifth year, palace guards Wang Yin, Liu Shao, Zhao Luan and others plotted rebellion; exposed, they were executed; their testimony implicated Duan Chang; Chang was removed from the privy council to prefect of Fen and strangled.

entries.zh: 乃以周廣順元年正月戊寅即皇帝位于太原，以子承鈞為太原尹，判官鄭珙、趙華為宰相，都押衙陳光裕為宣徽使，遣通事舍人李𧦬間行使于契丹。
entries.en: On the wuyin day of the first month of Guangshun 1, Min took the throne at Taiyuan, made Chengjun prefect of Taiyuan, appointed staff officers Zheng Qing and Zhao Hua as chancellors, named Chen Guangyu, chief military escort, Commissioner of the Palace Service, and sent Palace Communications Officer Li Gongyan as liaison envoy to the Khitan.
entries.literal: He then, on the wuyin day of the first month of the first year of Zhou Guangshun, took the throne at Taiyuan; appointed his son Chengjun governor of Taiyuan; made staff officers Zheng Qing and Zhao Hua chancellors; Chen Guangyu, chief military escort, Commissioner of the Palace Service; and sent Palace Communications Officer Li Gongyan as liaison envoy to the Khitan.

entries.zh: 契丹永康王兀欲與旻約為父子之國，旻乃遣宰相鄭珙致書兀欲，稱姪皇帝，以叔父事之而已。
entries.en: Khitan Prince of Eternal Peace Wuyu agreed with Min on a father-and-son state; Min sent Chancellor Zheng Qing to write Wuyu, styling himself Nephew Emperor and treating Wuyu only as uncle.
entries.literal: The Khitan Prince of Eternal Peace Wuyu agreed with Min on a father-and-son state relationship; Min then sent Chancellor Zheng Qing with a letter to Wuyu, styling himself Nephew Emperor and treating Wuyu only as uncle.

entries.zh: 兀欲遣燕王述軋、政事令高勳以冊尊旻為大漢神武皇帝，并冊旻妻為皇后。
entries.en: Wuyu sent Prince of Yan Shuzha and Director of Government Affairs Gao Xun with investiture documents to ennoble Min as Divine Martial Emperor of Great Han and Min's wife as empress.
entries.literal: Wuyu sent Prince of Yan Shuzha and Director of Government Affairs Gao Xun with documents to ennoble Min as Divine Martial Emperor of Great Han, and also to ennoble Min's wife as empress.

entries.zh: 兀欲性豪儁，漢使者至，輒以酒肉困之，珙素有疾，兀欲彊之飲，一夕而以醉卒。
entries.en: Wuyu was bold and convivial; whenever Han envoys came he overwhelmed them with food and wine. Qing had long been ill, but Wuyu forced him to drink, and he died drunk overnight.
entries.literal: Wuyu was by nature bold and free; whenever Han envoys arrived he wearied them with feasting; Qing had long been ill; Wuyu forced him to drink, and within a night he died drunk.

entries.zh: 然兀欲聞旻自立，頗幸中國多故，乃遣其貴臣述軋、高勳以自愛黃騮、九龍十二稻玉帶報聘。
entries.en: Yet when Wuyu heard Min had declared himself sovereign, he was pleased that the Central States were in turmoil and sent his honored ministers Shuzha and Gao Xun with his cherished yellow steed and a nine-dragon jade belt of twelve rice strands in return courtesy.
entries.literal: Yet hearing Min had declared himself sovereign, Wuyu was quite pleased that the Central States were beset with troubles, and sent his honored ministers Shuzha and Gao Xun with his cherished yellow steed and a jade belt of twelve rice strands with nine dragons in return courtesy.

entries.zh: 已而兀欲為述軋所弒，述律代立。
entries.en: Not long after, Wuyu was murdered by Shuzha, and Shulü came to the throne.
entries.literal: Before long Wuyu was assassinated by Shuzha, and Shulü succeeded him.

entries.zh: 旻遣樞密直學士王得中聘於述律，求兵以攻周。
entries.en: Min sent Privy Council academician Wang Dezong to Shulü to request troops against Zhou.
entries.literal: Min sent Academician Wang Dezong on an embassy to Shulü seeking troops to attack Zhou.

entries.zh: 述律遣蕭禹厥率兵五萬助旻。
entries.en: Shulü dispatched Xiao Yuque with fifty thousand men to aid him.
entries.literal: Shulü sent Xiao Yuque at the head of fifty thousand men to assist Min.

entries.zh: 旻出陰地攻晉州，為王峻所敗。
entries.en: Min raided from Yinzhou toward Jin Prefecture and was routed by Wang Jun.
entries.literal: Min advanced from Yin territory to attack Jin Prefecture and was defeated by Wang Jun.

entries.zh: 是歲大寒，旻軍凍餒，亡失過半。
entries.en: That winter was savage; hunger and frost claimed more than half his force.
entries.literal: That year the cold was extreme; Min's army suffered from cold and hunger, with more than half lost.

entries.zh: 明年，又攻府州，為折德扆所敗，德扆因取岢嵐軍。
entries.en: The following year he attacked Fu Prefecture, lost to She Deyi, who then seized Ke-lan garrison.
entries.literal: The next year he again attacked Fu Prefecture, was defeated by She Deyi; Deyi thereupon took Ke-lan Army.

entries.zh: 是時，世宗新即位，以謂旻幸周有大喪，而天子新立，必不能出兵，宜自將以擊其不意。
entries.en: The new Zhou emperor Chai Rong assumed Min would exploit the court's mourning and his own fresh accession—no army would come. He resolved to lead the campaign himself and surprise them.
entries.literal: At this time Shizong had just taken the throne; he judged that Min, seeing Zhou in great mourning and a new Son of Heaven, would be unable to march out, and that he himself ought to take the field to strike where they would not expect it.

entries.zh: 自宰相馮道等多言不可，世宗意甚銳。
entries.en: Feng Dao and others urged against it, but Shizong's mind was set.
entries.literal: Feng Dao and other ministers mostly said it could not be done, yet Shizong's resolve was very firm.

entries.zh: 顯德元年三月親征，甲午，戰於高平，李重進、白重贊將左，樊愛能、何徽將右，向訓、史彥超居中軍，張永德以禁兵衛蹕。
entries.en: Third month, Xiande 1: he marched in person. On jiawu day the armies met at Gaoping—Li Chongjin and Bai Chongzan on the left, Fan Aineng and He Hui on the right, Xiang Xun and Shi Yanchao in the center, Zhang Yongde shielding the imperial train with the palace guard.
entries.literal: In the third month of the first year of Xiande he led a personal expedition; on the jiawu day they fought at Gaoping. Li Chongjin and Bai Chongzan commanded the left, Fan Aineng and He Hui the right, Xiang Xun and Shi Yanchao the center, and Zhang Yongde guarded the imperial biao with the forbidden army.

entries.zh: 旻亦列為三陣，張元徽居東偏，楊袞居西偏，旻居其中。
entries.en: Min arrayed three corps—Yuanhui east, Yang Gun west, himself in the middle.
entries.literal: Min also drew up three lines: Zhang Yuanhui on the eastern wing, Yang Gun on the western, Min himself in the center.

entries.zh: 袞望周師謂旻曰：「敵也，未可輕動。」
entries.en: Yang Gun studied the Zhou lines and warned, "That is a real enemy—do not strike lightly."
entries.literal: Gun looked at the Zhou army and said to Min: "These are our foes—we must not move rashly."

entries.zh: 旻奮髯曰：「時不可失，無妄言也！」
entries.en: Min stroked his beard and snapped, "The hour will not wait—enough foolish talk!"
entries.literal: Min bristled his beard and said: "The moment must not be lost—do not talk nonsense!"

entries.zh: 衮怒而去。
entries.en: Gun stalked off in a rage.
entries.literal: Gun left in anger.

entries.zh: 旻號令東偏先進，王得中叩馬諫曰：「南風甚急，非北軍之利也，宜少待之。」
entries.en: Min ordered the eastern wing forward. Wang Dezong caught his bridle: "This fierce south wind favors the enemy—not us. Hold a while."
entries.literal: Min ordered the eastern wing to advance first; Wang Dezong seized his horse's bridle and remonstrated: "The south wind is very strong—not to the northern army's advantage; we ought to wait a little."

entries.zh: 旻怒曰：「老措大，毋妄沮吾軍！」
entries.en: Min snarled, "You old pedant—do not stammer at my host!"
entries.literal: Min raged: "Old bookworm—do not recklessly discourage my army!"

entries.zh: 即麾元徽，元徽擊周右軍，兵始交，愛能、徽退走，其騎軍亂，步卒數千棄甲叛降元徽，呼萬歲聲振川谷。
entries.en: He waved Yuanhui on. Yuanhui charged the Zhou right; at first clash Fan Aineng and He Hui fled; cavalry broke; thousands of infantry threw down arms and surrendered to Yuanhui, shouting "Long live!" till valleys echoed.
entries.literal: He immediately waved Yuanhui forward; Yuanhui struck Zhou's right wing; as the ranks met, Aineng and Hui retreated; their cavalry fell into disorder; several thousand foot soldiers cast off armor and surrendered to Yuanhui, crying ten thousand years till the valleys rang.

entries.zh: 世宗大駭，躬督戰士，士皆奮命爭先，而風勢愈盛，旻自麾赤幟收軍，軍不可遏，旻遂敗。
entries.en: Shizong was shaken but rode the line himself; men fought desperately; the wind rose fiercer still; Min waved red flags to recall his host—the host would not heed—Min was beaten.
entries.literal: Shizong was greatly alarmed and personally urged the warriors on; the soldiers all strove to be first; the wind grew still stronger; Min himself waved red banners to recall the army, but the army could not be stopped; Min was defeated.

entries.zh: 日暮，旻收余兵萬人阻澗而止。
entries.en: At dusk he rallied ten thousand survivors and barred a ravine to stand.
entries.literal: At dusk Min gathered the remaining ten thousand men and blocked the streambed to halt.

entries.zh: 是時，周之後軍，劉詞將之，在後未至，而世宗銳於速戰，戰已勝，詞軍繼至，因乘勝追擊之，旻又大敗，輜重器甲、乘輿服御物皆為周師所獲。
entries.en: Liu Ci's rearguard had not caught up; Shizong fought fast and won; then Ci arrived and pursued; Min suffered a second rout; wagons, armor, chariots, court dress, and imperial gear fell to Zhou.
entries.literal: At that time Zhou's rear guard under Liu Ci had not yet arrived; Shizong was keen on a quick battle; once victory was won, Ci's army came up and pressed the pursuit; Min was again heavily defeated; baggage, armor, carriages, robes, and imperial regalia were all taken by Zhou.

entries.zh: 旻獨乘契丹黃騮，自雕窠嶺間道馳去，夜失道山谷間，得村民為鄉導，誤趨平陽，得他道以歸，而張元徽戰歿於陣。
entries.en: Min alone fled on a yellow Khitan charger by mountain paths through Diaoke Ridge; night lost him in the hills until a farmer led him—wrongly toward Pingyang, then by another track home—while Yuanhui died on the field.
entries.literal: Min alone rode the Khitan yellow steed and fled by a path through Diaoke Ridge; at night he lost the way in the mountains; a villager guided him; he mistakenly hurried toward Pingyang; found another road and returned; Zhang Yuanhui fell in battle.

entries.zh: 楊袞怒旻，按兵西偏不戰，故獨全軍而返。
entries.en: Yang Gun, furious at Min, held the west wing idle and marched home whole.
entries.literal: Yang Gun was angry with Min; he held his western wing and did not fight, so his army alone returned intact.

entries.zh: 旻歸，為黃騮治廄，飾以金銀，食以三品料，號「自在將軍」。
entries.en: Back in Taiyuan he housed the horse in a gilded stable, fed it third-rank provender, and titled it "The Unfettered General."
entries.literal: When Min returned he built a stable for the yellow steed, adorned it with gold and silver, fed it third-rank rations, and styled it "General at Ease."

entries.zh: 世宗休軍潞州，大宴將士，斬敗將樊愛能、何徽等七十餘人，軍威大振。
entries.en: Shizong paused at Luzhou, banqueted his captains, and beheaded seventy-odd failed commanders, Fan and He among them; discipline surged.
entries.literal: Shizong rested the army at Luzhou and held a great feast for the commanders; he executed more than seventy defeated generals including Fan Aineng and He Hui; military awe was greatly increased.

entries.zh: 進攻太原，遣符彥卿、史彥超北控忻口，以斷契丹援路。
entries.en: He advanced on Taiyuan, posting Fu Yanqing and Shi Yanchao at Xin Ford to sever Khitan aid.
entries.literal: He pressed on toward Taiyuan, sent Fu Yanqing and Shi Yanchao north to hold Xin Ford and cut Khitan relief.

entries.zh: 太原城方四十里，周師去城三百步，圍之匝，自四月至於六月，攻之不克，而彥卿等為契丹所敗，彥超戰歿，世宗遽班師。
entries.en: The forty-li walls defied them from April through June; Yanqing's force was routed by Khitan; Yanchao fell; Shizong hurried south.
entries.literal: Taiyuan's walls measured forty li; Zhou encamped three hundred paces out and wrapped the city round; from the fourth month to the sixth month they assaulted without success; Yanqing and the rest were beaten by Khitan; Yanchao died in battle; Shizong withdrew in haste.

entries.zh: 初，周師圍城也，旻遣王得中送楊袞以歸，因乞援兵於契丹，契丹發數萬騎助旻，遣得中先還。
entries.en: Early in the siege Min sent Dezong to escort Yang Gun home and plead for reinforcements; Khitan dispatched tens of thousands and sent Dezong ahead.
entries.literal: When Zhou first besieged the city, Min had Wang Dezong escort Yang Gun home while begging more Khitan troops; Khitan sent tens of thousands of horse to help Min and sent Dezong back ahead.

entries.zh: 至代州，代州將桑珪殺防禦使鄭處謙，以城降周，並送得中於周。
entries.en: At Dai, General Sang Gui slew the defender Zheng Chuqian, yielded the city to Zhou, and delivered Dezong.
entries.literal: Reaching Dai Prefecture, its general Sang Gui killed Defender Zheng Chuqian, surrendered the city to Zhou, and handed Dezong to Zhou.

entries.zh: 世宗召問得中虜助兵多少，得中言送袞歸，無所求也，世宗信之。
entries.en: Shizong questioned Dezong on Khitan numbers; Dezong claimed he had only escorted Gun back—no aid asked—and was believed.
entries.literal: Shizong summoned and questioned Dezong how many Khitan auxiliaries there were; Dezong said escorting Gun home involved no request; Shizong believed him.

entries.zh: 已而契丹敗符彥卿於忻口，得中遂見殺。
entries.en: Khitan soon routed Fu Yanqing at Xin Ford; Dezong was executed.
entries.literal: Soon Khitan defeated Fu Yanqing at Xin Ford; Dezong was then killed.

entries.zh: 契丹遣高勛助承鈞，承鈞遣李存瑰與勛攻上黨，無所得而還。
entries.en: Khitan sent Gao Xun; Chengjun paired Li Cungui with him against Shangdang but gained nothing.
entries.literal: Khitan sent Gao Xun to aid Chengjun; Chengjun sent Li Cungui with Xun to attack Shangdang and returned empty-handed.

entries.zh: 明年，世宗北伐契丹，下三關，契丹使來告急，承鈞將發兵，而世宗班師，乃已。
entries.en: Next year Shizong marched on Khitan and seized three passes; urgent Khitan pleas moved Chengjun to mobilize—until Shizong retired and he stood down.
entries.literal: Next year Shizong campaigned north against Khitan, took three passes; Khitan sent urgent appeals; Chengjun was about to march out when Shizong withdrew and he stopped.

entries.zh: 宋興，昭義節度使李筠叛命，遣其將劉繼沖、判官孫孚奉表稱臣，執其監軍周光遜、李廷玉送於太原，乞兵為援。
entries.en: As Song began, Li Yun of Zhaoyi rebelled, sent Liu Jichong and Sun Fu to swear fealty, and delivered overseers Zhou Guangxun and Li Tingyu to Taiyuan for aid.
entries.literal: When Song rose, Zhaoyi governor Li Yun rebelled; he sent Liu Jichong and aide Sun Fu with a memorial of submission, handed his overseers Zhou Guangxun and Li Tingyu to Taiyuan, begging troops.

entries.zh: 承鈞欲謀於契丹，繼沖道筠意，請無用契丹兵。
entries.en: Chengjun meant to call on Khitan; Jichong conveyed Yun's plea to keep Khitan out.
entries.literal: Chengjun wished to consult Khitan; Jichong relayed Yun's wish to employ no Khitan troops.

entries.zh: 承鈞即率其國兵自將出團柏谷，群臣餞之汾水。
entries.en: He led his own army through Tuanbai Gorge while ministers toasted him on the Fen.
entries.literal: Chengjun thereupon led his native troops in person through Tuanbai Valley; the ministers saw him off at the Fen River.

entries.zh: 僕射趙華曰：「李筠舉事輕易，陛下不圖成敗，空國興師，臣實憂之。」
entries.en: Zhao Hua warned, "Yun acts rashly; you risk the realm without judging the odds—I fear disaster."
entries.literal: Vice Director Zhao Hua said: "Li Yun's uprising is rash; Your Majesty marches without weighing success—emptying the state—and I am deeply troubled."

entries.zh: 承鈞至太平驛，封筠隴西郡王。
entries.en: At Taiping Post he created Yun Duke of Longxi.
entries.literal: At Taiping Post Chengjun enfeoffed Yun as Duke of Longxi.

entries.zh: 筠見承鈞儀衛不備，非如王者，悔臣之，筠因自陳受周氏恩，不忍背德。
entries.en: Yun found Chengjun's train unkingly, repented his oath, and admitted Zhou's kindness left him unable to rebel.
entries.literal: Yun saw Chengjun's escort unfit for a king, regretted his submission, and confessed the Zhou had shown him kindness he could not betray.

entries.zh: 而承鈞與周世仇也，聞筠言亦不悅。
entries.en: Chengjun, Zhou's hereditary foe, took equal offense.
entries.literal: But Chengjun bore Zhou an inherited feud; hearing Yun he was displeased too.

entries.zh: 遣宣徽使盧贊監其軍，筠心益不平，與贊多不葉，承鈞遣宰相衛融和解之。
entries.en: He posted Lu Zan as supervisor; friction grew; Wei Rong was sent to patch peace.
entries.literal: He sent Commissioner Lu Zan to oversee Yun's army; Yun grew more resentful and clashed with Zan; Chengjun sent Chancellor Wei Rong to reconcile them.

entries.zh: 已而筠敗死，衛融被執至京師，太祖皇帝問融承鈞所以助筠反狀，融言不遜，太祖命以鐵楇擊其首，流血被面，融呼曰：「臣得死所矣！」
entries.en: Yun fell; Wei Rong was captured; Song's Taizu asked how Chengjun helped the revolt; Rong answered rudely; an iron maul split his brow; he shouted, "A worthy death!"
entries.literal: When Yun was defeated and killed, Wei Rong was seized and brought to the capital; Taizu asked what aid Chengjun had given Yun; Rong answered insolently; Taizu had an iron pestle strike his head until blood bathed his face; Rong cried: "I have found the place to die!"

entries.zh: 太祖顧左右曰：「此忠臣也。」
entries.en: Taizu told his men, "Here is loyalty."
entries.literal: Taizu looked to his attendants and said: "This is a loyal minister."

entries.zh: 釋之，命以良藥傅其瘡。
entries.en: He freed him and sent salves.
entries.literal: He released him and ordered good medicine applied to his wounds.

entries.zh: 遣融致書於承鈞，求周光遜等，約亦歸融太原。
entries.en: Rong carried a letter seeking Zhou Guangxun and company, offering to send Rong back too.
entries.literal: He sent Rong with a letter to Chengjun demanding Zhou Guangxun and others, promising Rong's return to Taiyuan as well.

entries.zh: 承鈞不報，融遂留京師。
entries.en: Chengjun did not answer; Rong remained.
entries.literal: Chengjun did not reply; Rong stayed at the capital.

entries.zh: 承鈞謂趙華曰：「不聽公言，幾至於敗。
entries.en: He told Zhao Hua, "Not heeding your words, I nearly came to ruin.
entries.literal: Chengjun said to Zhao Hua: "Not heeding your words, I nearly came to ruin.

entries.zh: 然失衛融、盧贊，吾以為恨爾。」
entries.en: but losing Rong and Zan grieves me."
entries.literal: Yet losing Wei Rong and Lu Zan—I regret it."

entries.zh: 或問：十國固非中國有也，然猶命以封爵，而稱中國年號來朝貢者，亦有之矣，本紀之不書，何也？
entries.en: Someone asked: The Ten Kingdoms were plainly not part of the central realm, yet some still received enfeoffments and came to court bearing tribute under the central dynasty's reign eras—why does the basic annals not record them?
entries.literal: Someone asked: The Ten Kingdoms were certainly not part of the Central Dynasty, yet some were still granted titles of nobility and came bearing tribute using the Central Dynasty's reign eras—why are these not recorded in the basic annals?

entries.zh: 曰：封爵之不書，所以見其非中國有也。
entries.en: The answer: That enfeoffments go unrecorded shows that these states did not belong to the central realm.
entries.literal: The reply: That enfeoffments are not recorded shows they were not part of the Central Dynasty.

entries.zh: 其朝貢之來如夷狄，以夷狄書之則甚矣。
entries.en: Their tribute missions came as those of barbarians would; to record them in the manner of barbarians would be going too far.
entries.literal: Their tribute missions came like those of the barbarians; to record them as barbarians would be excessive.

entries.zh: 問者曰：四夷、十國，皆非中國之有也，四夷之封爵朝貢則書，而十國之不書何也？
entries.en: The questioner said: The Four Barbarians and the Ten Kingdoms alike did not belong to the central realm—why record the enfeoffments and tribute of the Four Barbarians but not those of the Ten Kingdoms?
entries.literal: The questioner said: The Four Barbarians and the Ten Kingdoms were none of them part of the Central Dynasty—why record the Four Barbarians' enfeoffments and tribute but not the Ten Kingdoms'?

entries.zh: 曰：以中國而視夷狄，夷狄之可也。
entries.en: The answer: To regard the barbarians from the standpoint of the central court is permissible.
entries.literal: The reply: To view the barbarians from the standpoint of the Central Dynasty is permissible.

entries.zh: 以五代之君而視十國，夷狄之則未可也。
entries.en: For the rulers of the Five Dynasties to treat the Ten Kingdoms as barbarians is not permissible.
entries.literal: For the rulers of the Five Dynasties to view the Ten Kingdoms as barbarians is not permissible.

entries.zh: 故十國之封爵、朝貢，不如夷狄，則無以書之。
entries.en: Therefore the enfeoffments and tribute of the Ten Kingdoms, being beneath those of the barbarians in standing, cannot be recorded.
entries.literal: Therefore the enfeoffments and tribute of the Ten Kingdoms, being inferior to those of the barbarians, cannot be recorded.

entries.zh: 書如夷狄，則五代之君未可以夷狄之也。
entries.en: To record them as barbarians would mean that the rulers of the Five Dynasties could not treat them as barbarians.
entries.literal: To record them as barbarians would mean the rulers of the Five Dynasties could not treat them as barbarians.

entries.zh: 是以外而不書，見其自絕於中國焉爾。
entries.en: Hence they are placed outside the record and left unwritten, showing that they had cut themselves off from the central realm.
entries.literal: Hence they are set outside and not recorded, showing how they cut themselves off from the Central Dynasty.

entries.zh: 問者曰：外而不書，則東漢之立何以書？
entries.en: The questioner said: If they are set outside and not recorded, then why is the founding of Eastern Han recorded?
entries.literal: The questioner said: If set outside and not recorded, then why record the establishment of Eastern Han?

entries.zh: 曰：吾於東漢，常異其辭於九國也。
entries.en: The answer: In my treatment of Eastern Han I consistently use wording distinct from that applied to the other nine states.
entries.literal: The reply: In my treatment of Eastern Han I consistently use wording distinct from that for the Nine States.

entries.zh: 《春秋》因亂世而立治法，本紀以治法而正亂君。
entries.en: The Spring and Autumn Annals established governing principles amid an age of chaos; the basic annals employ those principles to set right unruly rulers.
entries.literal: The Spring and Autumn Annals established governing principles amid chaotic times; the basic annals use governing principles to rectify unruly rulers.

entries.zh: 世亂則疑難之事多，正疑處難，敢不慎也。
entries.en: When the age is chaotic, doubtful matters multiply; to resolve doubts amid difficulty—how could one fail to be cautious?
entries.literal: When the age is chaotic, doubtful matters multiply; to resolve doubts in difficulty—how could one not be cautious?

entries.zh: 周、漢之事，可謂難矣哉！
entries.en: The affairs of the Zhou and Han states may truly be called difficult!
entries.literal: The affairs of Zhou and Han may truly be called difficult!

entries.zh: 或謂：劉旻嘗致書於周，求其子赟不得而後自立，然則旻之志不以忘漢為仇，而以失子為仇也。
entries.en: Some argue that Liu Min once sent a letter to the Zhou court seeking the return of his son Yun and only afterward established himself on his own; on this view Min's motive was not enmity toward those who had abandoned Han but enmity over the loss of his son.
entries.literal: Some say Liu Min once sent a letter to Zhou seeking his son Yun and only afterward established himself independently; then Min's intent was not to treat forgetting Han as enmity but losing his son as enmity.

entries.zh: 曰：漢嘗詔立赟為嗣，則赟為漢之國君，不獨為旻子也。
entries.en: The answer: Han had once issued an edict establishing Yun as heir; Yun was Han's sovereign, not merely Min's son.
entries.literal: The reply: Han once issued an edict establishing Yun as heir; Yun was Han's sovereign, not merely Min's son.

entries.zh: 旻之大義，宜不為周屈，其立雖未必是，而義當不屈於周，此其可以異乎九國矣。
entries.en: By the standard of great righteousness Min ought not to have bowed to Zhou; though his establishing himself may not have been correct in every respect, righteousness required that he not submit to Zhou—here he may be distinguished from the other nine states.
entries.literal: Min's great righteousness ought not submit to Zhou; though his establishing himself may not necessarily have been right, righteousness demanded he not submit to Zhou—this is where he may be distinguished from the Nine States.

entries.zh: 終旻之世，猶稱乾祐，至承鈞立，然後改元，則旻之志豈不可哀也哉！
entries.en: Throughout Min's life he still used the Qianyou reign era; only when Cheng Jun succeeded did the state change its era name—how lamentable was Min's resolve!
entries.literal: Through Min's entire life he still used the Qianyou era; only when Cheng Jun succeeded did he change the era—how lamentable was Min's resolve!

entries.zh: 〈（十國年世，惟楚、閩、東漢三國，諸家之說不同，而互有得失，最難考正。
entries.en: (Among the chronologies of the Ten Kingdoms, only Chu, Min, and Eastern Han present differing accounts in the various sources, each with its strengths and flaws—these are the hardest to verify.
entries.literal: (Among the chronologies of the Ten Kingdoms, only Chu, Min, and Eastern Han have differing accounts among various sources, each with mutual gains and losses—hardest to verify.

entries.zh: 今略其諸說而正其是者，庶幾博覽者不惑，而一以《年譜》為正也。
entries.en: Here I briefly set aside the various accounts and correct what is sound, so that readers may not be misled and may take this Timeline as the standard.
entries.literal: Now I briefly set aside the various accounts and correct what is right, so that broad readers may not be confused and may take the Timeline as authoritative.

entries.zh: 馬氏，據《湖湘故事》、《九國志》、《運歷圖》，並雲殷以長興元年卒，是歲，子希聲立，長興三年卒。
entries.en: For the Ma clan of Chu: according to the Huxiang Gushi, the Jiuguo Zhi, and the Yunli Tu, all agree that Yin died in the first year of Changxing; that year his son Xisheng succeeded, and Xisheng died in the third year of Changxing.
entries.literal: The Ma clan: according to the Huxiang Gushi, Jiuguo Zhi, and Yunli Tu, all say Yin died in the first year of Changxing; that year his son Xisheng succeeded; he died in the third year of Changxing.

entries.zh: 而《五代舊史》殷列傳云，殷長興二年卒，享年七十八，子希聲立，不周歲而卒；
entries.en: But the biography of Yin in the Old History of the Five Dynasties says he died in the second year of Changxing at the age of seventy-eight, that his son Xisheng succeeded him, and that Xisheng died within a year;
entries.literal: But the biography of Yin in the Old History of the Five Dynasties says Yin died in the second year of Changxing, aged seventy-eight; his son Xisheng succeeded and died within a year;

entries.zh: 明宗本紀長興元年，書希聲除節度使，起復，三年八月，又書希聲卒。
entries.en: The annals of Emperor Mingzong for the first year of Changxing record Xisheng's appointment as military commissioner, resuming office from mourning leave; in the eighth month of the third year they again record Xisheng's death.
entries.literal: The annals of Emperor Mingzong for the first year of Changxing record Xisheng appointed military commissioner, resuming office from mourning; in the eighth month of the third year they again record Xisheng's death.

entries.zh: 今據《九國志》，殷以大中六年歲在壬申生，享年七十九。
entries.en: According to the Jiuguo Zhi, Yin was born in the sixth year of Dazhong (the renshen year) and died at the age of seventy-nine.
entries.literal: Now according to the Jiuguo Zhi, Yin was born in the sixth year of Dazhong, the year renshen, and died aged seventy-nine.

entries.zh: 蓋自大中壬申至長興元年庚寅，實七十九年，為得其實。
entries.en: From the renshen year of Dazhong to the gengyin year of the first year of Changxing is in fact seventy-nine years—this is the correct figure.
entries.literal: From Dazhong renshen to the first year of Changxing gengyin is truly seventy-nine years—this is correct.

entries.zh: 而希聲，據《湖湘故事》、《九國志》、《運歷圖》皆以三年卒，與明宗本紀皆合，不疑。
entries.en: As for Xisheng, the Huxiang Gushi, the Jiuguo Zhi, and the Yunli Tu all place his death in the third year, which agrees with the annals of Mingzong—there is no doubt here.
entries.literal: As for Xisheng, the Huxiang Gushi, Jiuguo Zhi, and Yunli Tu all say he died in the third year, matching the annals of Mingzong—no doubt.

entries.zh: 惟《舊史》書殷卒二年，及年七十八，希聲立不周歲卒為繆爾。
entries.en: Only the Old History's claim that Yin died in the second year at the age of seventy-eight and that Xisheng died within a year of succeeding is mistaken.
entries.literal: Only the Old History's recording Yin dying in the second year, aged seventy-eight, and Xisheng dying within a year of succession is in error.

entries.zh: 希萼、希崇之亂，南唐盡遷馬氏之族歸於金陵。
entries.en: During the turmoil of Xi'e and Xichong, Southern Tang relocated the entire Ma clan to Jinling.
entries.literal: In the turmoil of Xi'e and Xichong, Southern Tang moved the entire Ma clan to Jinling.

entries.zh: 《五代舊史》云，時廣順元年也。
entries.en: The Old History of the Five Dynasties says this occurred in the first year of Guangshun.
entries.literal: The Old History of the Five Dynasties says this was in the first year of Guangshun.

entries.zh: 而《運歷圖》雲乾祐二年馬氏滅者，繆也。
entries.en: But the Yunli Tu's claim that the Ma clan was destroyed in the second year of Qianyou is mistaken.
entries.literal: But the Yunli Tu's saying the Ma clan was destroyed in the second year of Qianyou is in error.

entries.zh: 初，殷入湖南，掘地得石，讖云：「龍起頭，豬掉尾。」
entries.en: When Yin first entered Hunan, he dug up a stone bearing a prophecy that read: "The dragon rises at the head, the pig drops at the tail."
entries.literal: Initially, when Yin entered Hunan, he dug up a stone with a prophecy that read: "The dragon rises at the head, the pig drops at the tail."

entries.zh: 蓋殷以乾寧三年歲在丙辰，自立於湖南，至廣順元年辛亥而滅。
entries.en: For Yin established himself in Hunan in the third year of Qianning (the bingchen year) and was destroyed in the first year of Guangshun (the xinhai year).
entries.literal: For Yin established himself in Hunan in the third year of Qianning, the year bingchen, and was destroyed in the first year of Guangshun, xinhai.

entries.zh: 《九國志》以乾祐三年為辛亥，《湖湘故事》以顯德元年為辛亥者，皆繆也。
entries.en: The Jiuguo Zhi's identification of the third year of Qianyou as the xinhai year and the Huxiang Gushi's identification of the first year of Xiande as xinhai are both mistaken.
entries.literal: The Jiuguo Zhi's taking the third year of Qianyou as xinhai and the Huxiang Gushi's taking the first year of Xiande as xinhai are both in error.

entries.zh: 惟《五代舊史》得其實。
entries.en: Only the Old History of the Five Dynasties has the correct date.
entries.literal: Only the Old History of the Five Dynasties got it right.

entries.zh: 王氏世次，曰潮、曰審知、曰延翰、曰璘、曰昶、曰曦、曰延政，凡七主。
entries.en: The Wang clan succession runs: Chao, Shenzhi, Yanhan, Lin, Chang, Xi, and Yanzheng—seven rulers in all.
entries.literal: The succession of the Wang clan runs: Chao, Shenzhi, Yanhan, Lin, Chang, Xi, Yanzheng—seven rulers in all.

entries.zh: 而潮以唐景福元年歲在壬子始入福州，至開運三年丙午而滅，實五十五年。
entries.en: Chao entered Fuzhou in the first year of Jingfu of Tang (the renzi year), and the clan was destroyed in the third year of Kaiyun (the bingwu year)—fifty-five years in all.
entries.literal: Chao entered Fuzhou in the first year of Jingfu of Tang, the year renzi, and the clan was destroyed in the third year of Kaiyun, bingwu—truly fifty-five years.

entries.zh: 當云七主五十五年，為得其實。
entries.en: The correct figure is seven rulers over fifty-five years.
entries.literal: It should read seven rulers and fifty-five years—this is correct.

entries.zh: 而《運歷圖》雲五十六年，《九國志》、《五代舊史》、《紀年通譜》、《閩中實錄》、《閩王列傳》皆云七主六十年者，皆繆也。
entries.en: But the Yunli Tu gives fifty-six years, and the Jiuguo Zhi, the Old History of the Five Dynasties, the Jinian Tongpu, the Minzhong Shilu, and the Min Wang Liezhuan all give seven rulers over sixty years—these are all mistaken.
entries.literal: But the Yunli Tu says fifty-six years; the Jiuguo Zhi, Old History of the Five Dynasties, Jinian Tongpu, Minzhong Shilu, and Min Wang Liezhuan all say seven rulers and sixty years—these are all in error.

entries.zh: 審知，《五代舊史》本傳云，同光元年十二月卒，《九國志》亦云同光元年卒。
entries.en: For Shenzhi, the biography in the Old History of the Five Dynasties says he died in the twelfth month of the first year of Tongguang; the Jiuguo Zhi likewise places his death in the first year of Tongguang.
entries.literal: Shenzhi: the biography in the Old History of the Five Dynasties says he died in the twelfth month of the first year of Tongguang; the Jiuguo Zhi also says he died in the first year of Tongguang.

entries.zh: 《運歷圖》同光三年卒。
entries.en: The Yunli Tu places his death in the third year of Tongguang.
entries.literal: The Yunli Tu says he died in the third year of Tongguang.

entries.zh: 今檢《五代舊史》莊宗本紀，同光二年五月丙午，審知加檢校太師守中書令，豈得卒於元年也？
entries.en: Checking the annals of Emperor Zhuangzong in the Old History of the Five Dynasties: in the fifth month of the second year of Tongguang (bingwu day), Shenzhi was promoted to acting Grand Preceptor and concurrent Director of the Secretariat—how could he have died in the first year?
entries.literal: Now checking the annals of Emperor Zhuangzong in the Old History of the Five Dynasties: in the fifth month of the second year of Tongguang, bingwu, Shenzhi was promoted to acting Grand Preceptor and concurrent Director of the Secretariat—how could he have died in the first year?

entries.zh: 又至四年二月庚子，福建副使王延翰奏稱權知軍府事，三月辛亥，遂除延翰威武軍節度使。
entries.en: Further, in the second month of the fourth year (gengzi day), the Fujian deputy commissioner Wang Yanhan reported that he was acting military governor; in the third month (xinhai day), Yanhan was appointed military commissioner of the Weiwu Army.
entries.literal: Further, in the second month of the fourth year, gengzi, the Fujian deputy commissioner Wang Yanhan reported that he was acting military governor; in the third month, xinhai, Yanhan was appointed military commissioner of the Weiwu Army.

entries.zh: 以此推之，審知卒當在同光三年十二月，蓋閩去京師遠，明年二月延翰之奏始至京師，理當然也。
entries.en: From this we infer that Shenzhi died in the twelfth month of the third year of Tongguang; Min lies far from the capital, so Yanhan's report reached the capital only in the second month of the following year—which is only to be expected.
entries.literal: From this we infer Shenzhi died in the twelfth month of the third year of Tongguang; Min is far from the capital, so Yanhan's report reached the capital only in the second month of the following year—as reason demands.

entries.zh: 又據《閩王列傳》、《九國志》，皆云審知在位二十九年。
entries.en: According to the Min Wang Liezhuan and the Jiuguo Zhi, both state that Shenzhi reigned twenty-nine years.
entries.literal: Further, according to the Min Wang Liezhuan and Jiuguo Zhi, both say Shenzhi reigned twenty-nine years.

entries.zh: 審知以唐乾寧四年嗣位，是歲丁巳，至同光三年乙酉，實二十九年。
entries.en: Shenzhi succeeded in the fourth year of Qianning of Tang (the dingsi year) and reigned until the third year of Tongguang (the yiyou year)—twenty-nine years in all.
entries.literal: Shenzhi succeeded in the fourth year of Qianning of Tang, the year dingsi, to the third year of Tongguang, yiyou—truly twenty-nine years.

entries.zh: 則《運歷圖》為是，而《舊史》、《九國志》元年卒者，皆繆也。
entries.en: Thus the Yunli Tu is correct, while the Old History and the Jiuguo Zhi, which place his death in the first year, are mistaken.
entries.literal: Thus the Yunli Tu is correct, while the Old History and Jiuguo Zhi's first-year death dates are in error.

entries.zh: 璘本名延鈞，《五代舊史》本傳云在位十二年。
entries.en: Lin, whose original name was Yanjun: the biography in the Old History of the Five Dynasties says he reigned twelve years.
entries.literal: Lin, whose original name was Yanjun: the biography in the Old History of the Five Dynasties says he reigned twelve years.

entries.zh: 《九國志》云在位十一年。
entries.en: The Jiuguo Zhi says he reigned eleven years.
entries.literal: The Jiuguo Zhi says he reigned eleven years.

entries.zh: 《閩王列傳》、《紀年通譜》皆云在位十年。
entries.en: The Min Wang Liezhuan and the Jinian Tongpu both say he reigned ten years.
entries.literal: The Min Wang Liezhuan and Jinian Tongpu both say he reigned ten years.

entries.zh: 蓋璘以天成元年殺延翰自立，是歲丙戌，至清泰二年乙未，實十年而卒，與《閩王列傳》合，而《舊史》、《九國志》皆繆也。
entries.en: Lin killed Yanhan and established himself in the first year of Tiancheng (the bingxu year) and died in the second year of Qingtai (the yimao year)—ten years in all, which agrees with the Min Wang Liezhuan; the Old History and the Jiuguo Zhi are mistaken.
entries.literal: Lin killed Yanhan and established himself in the first year of Tiancheng, the year bingxu, and died in the second year of Qingtai, yimao—truly ten years, matching the Min Wang Liezhuan; the Old History and Jiuguo Zhi are in error.

entries.zh: 璘以清泰二年改元永和，是歲見殺，而《舊史》、《九國志》、《運歷圖》皆無永和之號，又《運歷圖》書鏻見殺在天福元年丙申者，皆繆也。
entries.en: Lin changed the era name to Yonghe in the second year of Qingtai and was killed that same year; yet the Old History, the Jiuguo Zhi, and the Yunli Tu all omit the Yonghe era name, and the Yunli Tu's claim that Lin was killed in the first year of Tianfu (the bingshen year) is likewise mistaken.
entries.literal: Lin changed the era to Yonghe in the second year of Qingtai and was killed that year; yet the Old History, Jiuguo Zhi, and Yunli Tu all lack the Yonghe era name, and the Yunli Tu's recording Lin killed in the first year of Tianfu, bingshen, is also in error.

entries.zh: 劉旻，《九國志》云，乾祐七年十一月旻卒，享年六十，子承鈞立，時年二十九。
entries.en: For Liu Min, the Jiuguo Zhi says that in the eleventh month of the seventh year of Qianyou Min died at the age of sixty and his son Cheng Jun succeeded at the age of twenty-nine.
entries.literal: Liu Min: the Jiuguo Zhi says in the eleventh month of the seventh year of Qianyou Min died, aged sixty; his son Cheng Jun succeeded, aged twenty-nine.

entries.zh: 乾祐七年，乃顯德元年也。
entries.en: The seventh year of Qianyou corresponds to the first year of Xiande.
entries.literal: The seventh year of Qianyou is the first year of Xiande.

entries.zh: 而《五代舊史》、《周世宗實錄》、《運歷圖》、《紀年通譜》皆云顯德二年冬旻卒。
entries.en: But the Old History of the Five Dynasties, the Shilu of Emperor Shizong of Zhou, the Yunli Tu, and the Jinian Tongpu all place Min's death in the winter of the second year of Xiande.
entries.literal: But the Old History of the Five Dynasties, Shilu of Emperor Shizong of Zhou, Yunli Tu, and Jinian Tongpu all say Min died in the winter of the second year of Xiande.

entries.zh: 又有旻偽中書舍人王保衡《晉陽見聞要錄》雲，旻乙卯生，卒年六十一，子承鈞立。
entries.en: There is also the Jinyang Jianwen Yaolu by Wang Baoheng, a Secretariat drafter in Min's court, which says Min was born in the yimao year, died at the age of sixty-one, and was succeeded by his son Cheng Jun.
entries.literal: There is also the Jinyang Jianwen Yaolu by Wang Baoheng, Min's false Secretariat Drafter, which says Min was born in yimao, died aged sixty-one, and his son Cheng Jun succeeded.

entries.zh: 承鈞丙戌生，立時年二十九。
entries.en: Cheng Jun was born in the bingxu year and was twenty-nine when he succeeded.
entries.literal: Cheng Jun was born in bingxu and was twenty-nine when he succeeded.

entries.zh: 保衡是旻之臣，其親所見聞，所得最實，然而頗為轉寫差誤爾。
entries.en: Baoheng was Min's minister; what he witnessed firsthand is the most reliable account, yet it has suffered considerable errors in transmission.
entries.literal: Baoheng was Min's minister; what he personally saw and heard is the most reliable, yet it has suffered considerable copying errors.

entries.zh: 按保衡書旻乙卯生，若享年六十一，當於乙卯歲卒，則是顯德二年也。
entries.en: According to Baoheng's record, Min was born in the yimao year; if he died at the age of sixty-one, he should have died in a yimao year—which would be the second year of Xiande.
entries.literal: According to Baoheng's record, Min was born in yimao; if he died aged sixty-one, he should have died in the yimao year—which would be the second year of Xiande.

entries.zh: 又書承鈞丙戌生，立時年二十九，則當是顯德元年甲寅歲也。
entries.en: It also records that Cheng Jun was born in the bingxu year and was twenty-nine at succession—which would place his accession in the jiayin year, the first year of Xiande.
entries.literal: It also records Cheng Jun born in bingxu and twenty-nine at succession—this should be the jiayin year, the first year of Xiande.

entries.zh: 豈有旻卒於二年，承鈞以元年嗣位？
entries.en: How could Min have died in the second year while Cheng Jun succeeded in the first?
entries.literal: How could Min die in the second year while Cheng Jun succeeded in the first year?

entries.zh: 理必不然。
entries.en: That cannot be right.
entries.literal: Reason demands this cannot be so.

entries.zh: 以《九國志》參較，旻享年六十，顯德元年卒，承鈞以是歲嗣位，時年二十九，為得其實，但《見聞要錄》衍「一」字爾。
entries.en: Compared with the Jiuguo Zhi, Min died at sixty in the first year of Xiande and Cheng Jun succeeded that same year at twenty-nine—this is the correct account; the Jianwen Yaolu merely added a spurious character for "one."
entries.literal: Comparing with the Jiuguo Zhi, Min died aged sixty in the first year of Xiande; Cheng Jun succeeded that year aged twenty-nine—this is correct; only the Jianwen Yaolu added a spurious "one" character.

entries.zh: 其云二年卒者，皆繆也。
entries.en: Those who place his death in the second year are all mistaken.
entries.literal: Those saying he died in the second year are all in error.

entries.zh: 《九國志》又云，承鈞立，服喪三年，至乾祐九年服除，改十年為天會元年，當是顯德四年。
entries.en: The Jiuguo Zhi also records that when Cheng Jun succeeded he observed three years of mourning; in the ninth year of Qianyou the mourning period ended and the tenth year was renamed the first year of Tianhui—which corresponds to the fourth year of Xiande.
entries.literal: The Jiuguo Zhi also says: when Cheng Jun succeeded, he observed three years of mourning; in the ninth year of Qianyou mourning ended and the tenth year was changed to the first year of Tianhui—which should be the fourth year of Xiande.

entries.zh: 而《紀年通譜》以顯德三年為天會元年者，繆也。
entries.en: But the Jinian Tongpu's identification of the third year of Xiande as the first year of Tianhui is mistaken.
entries.literal: But the Jinian Tongpu's taking the third year of Xiande as the first year of Tianhui is in error.

entries.zh: 晉與梁為敵國，自稱天祐者二十年，故首列於《年譜》，其後遂滅梁而為唐，故不列於世家。）〉
entries.en: Jin and Liang were rival states; Jin used the Tianyou era name for twenty years, so it is listed first in the Timeline; afterward it destroyed Liang and became Tang, and therefore is not included among the hereditary houses.)〉
entries.literal: Jin and Liang were enemy states; Jin called itself Tianyou for twenty years, so it is listed first in the Timeline; afterward it destroyed Liang and became Tang, so it is not listed among the hereditary houses.)〉

entries.zh: 嗚呼，堯、舜盛矣！
entries.en: Alas, how magnificent were Yao and Shun!
entries.literal: Alas, how flourishing were Yao and Shun!

entries.zh: 三代之王，功有餘而德不足，故皆更始以自新，由是改正朔矣，至於後世，遂名年以建元。
entries.en: The kings of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou had accomplished much but lacked sufficient virtue, so each renewed his rule to make a fresh start. From this arose the reform of the calendar; in later ages, rulers came to name the years of their reigns to mark the beginning of a new era.
entries.literal: The kings of the Three Dynasties had merit in surplus but virtue insufficient; therefore all renewed their beginnings to reform themselves. Thereby they changed the calendar; reaching later ages, they then named years to establish reign eras.

entries.zh: 及僭竊交興，而稱號紛雜，則不可以不別也。
entries.en: Once usurpations arose one after another and titles grew tangled and confused, they had to be distinguished.
entries.literal: When usurpations arose in succession and titles became confused and mixed, they could not but be distinguished.

entries.zh: 五代十國，稱帝改元者七。
entries.en: Among the states of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, seven declared themselves emperors and established new reign eras.
entries.literal: Of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, seven declared themselves emperors and changed their reign eras.

entries.zh: 吳越、荊、楚，常行中國年號。
entries.en: Wu-Yue, Jingnan, and Chu ordinarily followed the reign eras of the central court.
entries.literal: Wu-Yue, Jing, and Chu ordinarily used the reign eras of the Central Dynasty.

entries.zh: 然予聞於故老，謂吳越亦嘗稱帝改元，而求其事跡不可得，頗疑吳越後自諱之。
entries.en: Yet I have heard from old men that Wu-Yue too once declared itself emperor and changed its era name, though the particulars cannot be recovered; I rather suspect that Wu-Yue later suppressed the record on its own account.
entries.literal: Yet I have heard from elders that Wu-Yue also once declared itself emperor and changed its reign era, but the particulars cannot be found; I rather suspect that Wu-Yue later concealed this of its own accord.

entries.zh: 及旁采閩、楚、南漢諸國之書，與吳越往來者多矣，皆無稱帝之事。
entries.en: When I collected materials from the records of Min, Chu, Southern Han, and the other states—many of which record dealings with Wu-Yue—none mention Wu-Yue's having claimed the imperial title.
entries.literal: When I gathered materials from the books of Min, Chu, Southern Han, and other states—there are many dealings with Wu-Yue—none mention their claiming imperial title.

entries.zh: 獨得其封落星石為寶石山制書，稱寶正六年辛卯，則知其嘗改元矣。
entries.en: Only in an imperial edict enfeoffing the Falling Star Stone as Baoshi Mountain, dated to the sixth year of Baozheng (xinmao), do we learn that they once established a new reign era.
entries.literal: Only in finding an imperial edict bestowing the Falling Star Stone as Baoshi Mountain, dated to the sixth year of Baozheng, xinmao, do we know that they once changed their reign era.

entries.zh: 辛卯，長興二年，乃镠之末世也，然不見其終始所因，故不得而備列。
entries.en: Xinmao corresponds to the second year of the Changxing era, the last years of Qian Liu's reign; but because the beginning and end of the matter are nowhere recorded, it cannot be set forth in full.
entries.literal: Xinmao is the second year of Changxing, the last age of Liu; yet without seeing the beginning and end of the matter, it cannot be fully listed.

entries.zh: 錢氏訖五代，嘗外尊中國，豈其張軌之比乎。
entries.en: Throughout the Five Dynasties the Qian clan outwardly honored the central court—were they not comparable to Zhang Gui?
entries.literal: The Qian clan through the Five Dynasties outwardly honored the Central Dynasty—were they not comparable to Zhang Gui?

entries.zh: 十國皆非中國有也，其稱帝改元與不，未足較其得失，故並列之。
entries.en: None of the Ten Kingdoms truly belonged to the central realm; whether a state declared itself emperor and changed its era name is not enough to judge its merits and faults, so I list them together.
entries.literal: None of the Ten Kingdoms properly belonged to the Central Dynasty; whether they declared emperorship and changed eras is insufficient ground to weigh their merits and faults, so they are listed together.

entries.zh: 作《十國世家年譜》。
entries.en: Thus I composed the "Timeline for the Hereditary Houses of the Ten Kingdoms."
entries.literal: I composed the "Timeline for the Hereditary Houses of the Ten Kingdoms."

entries.zh: 莊宗討張文禮，圍鎮州。
entries.en: Zhuangzong campaigned against Zhang Wenli and besieged Zhenzhou.
entries.literal: Zhuangzong campaigned against Zhang Wenli and besieged Zhenzhou.

entries.zh: 定州王處直懼鎮且亡，晉兵必並擊己，遣其子郁說契丹，使入塞以牽晉兵。
entries.en: Wang Chuzhi of Dingzhou feared that once Zhen fell, Jin armies would turn on him. He sent his son Yu to urge the Khitan to raid the border and draw Jin forces away.
entries.literal: Dingzhou's Wang Chuzhi feared Zhen would soon perish and Jin troops would jointly strike him; he sent his son Yu to persuade the Khitan to enter the passes and pull Jin troops away.

entries.zh: 郁謂阿保機曰：「臣父處直使布愚款曰：故趙王王镕，王趙六世，鎮州金城湯池，金帛山積，燕姬趙女，羅綺盈廷。
entries.en: Yu told Abaoji, "My father Chuzhi sends his humble pledge: the late King of Zhao, Wang Rong, held Zhao for six generations. Zhenzhou is a fortress of gold and boiling moats, with treasure heaped like mountains, Yan and Zhao beauties, and silks filling the halls.
entries.literal: Yu said to Abaoji: "My father Chuzhi sends me to lay out a foolish sincerity, saying: the former King of Zhao Wang Rong ruled Zhao six generations; Zhenzhou is golden city and boiling moat, gold and silks piled like mountains, Yan maidens and Zhao women, gauze and silk filling the hall.

entries.zh: 張文禮得之而為晉所攻，懼死不暇，故皆留以待皇帝。」
entries.en: Zhang Wenli seized it all but is now besieged by Jin and too terrified for his life to keep it—everything waits for Your Majesty."
entries.literal: Zhang Wenli obtained it and is attacked by Jin; fearing death he has no leisure—therefore all is left awaiting Your Majesty.

entries.zh: 阿保機大喜。
entries.en: Abaoji was delighted.
entries.literal: Abaoji was greatly pleased.

entries.zh: 其妻述律不肯，曰：「我有羊馬之富，西樓足以娛樂，今舍此而遠赴人之急，我聞晉兵強天下，且戰有勝敗，後悔何追？」
entries.en: His wife Shulü objected: "We have flocks and herds in plenty, and the Western Tower is amusement enough. Why leave this and rush to another's crisis? I hear Jin armies are the strongest under heaven—and battles have winners and losers. What use is regret afterward?"
entries.literal: His wife Shulü would not agree, saying: "I have the wealth of sheep and horses; the Western Tower suffices for pleasure—now to abandon this and go far to another's urgency; I hear Jin troops are strongest under heaven, and moreover in battle there is victory and defeat—what regret can be pursued afterward?

entries.zh: 阿保機躍然曰：「張文禮有金玉百萬，留待皇后，可共取之。」
entries.en: Abaoji sprang up and said, "Zhang Wenli has millions in gold and jade set aside for the Queen—you and I can take it together."
entries.literal: Abaoji leaped up and said: "Zhang Wenli has a million in gold and jade left awaiting the Queen—you may take it together."

entries.zh: 於是空國入寇。
entries.en: He then led the whole nation on an invasion.
entries.literal: Thereupon he emptied the state and entered to raid.

entries.zh: 郁之召契丹也，定人皆以為後患不可召，而處直不聽。
entries.en: When Yu summoned the Khitan, everyone in Dingzhou warned that this would bring future disaster, but Chuzhi would not listen.
entries.literal: In Yu's summoning of the Khitan, the people of Ding all considered it a later calamity and that they must not be summoned, but Chuzhi would not listen.

entries.zh: 郁已去，處直為其子都所廢。
entries.en: After Yu departed, Chuzhi was overthrown by his son Du.
entries.literal: After Yu had gone, Chuzhi was deposed by his son Du.

entries.zh: 阿保機攻幽州不克，又攻涿州，陷之。
entries.en: Abaoji failed to take Youzhou, then attacked Zhuozhou and captured it.
entries.literal: Abaoji attacked Youzhou without taking it, then attacked Zhuozhou and captured it.

entries.zh: 聞處直廢而都立，遂攻中山，渡沙河。
entries.en: Learning that Chuzhi had been deposed and Du installed, he marched on Zhongshan and crossed the Sha River.
entries.literal: Hearing Chuzhi was deposed and Du established, he then attacked Zhongshan and crossed the Sha River.

entries.zh: 都告急於莊宗。
entries.en: Du sent an urgent appeal to Zhuangzong.
entries.literal: Du reported urgency to Zhuangzong.

entries.zh: 莊宗自將鐵騎五千，遇契丹前鋒於新城，晉兵自桑林馳出，人馬精甲，光明燭日。
entries.en: Zhuangzong led five thousand armored horsemen in person and met the Khitan vanguard at Xincheng. Jin troops burst from Sanglin—men and horses in gleaming armor, light blazing like the sun.
entries.literal: Zhuangzong personally led five thousand iron cavalry, met the Khitan vanguard at Xincheng; Jin troops burst out from Sanglin, men and horses in fine armor, brightness illuminating the sun.

entries.zh: 虜騎愕然，稍卻，晉軍乘之，虜遂散走，而沙河冰薄，虜皆陷沒。
entries.en: The enemy cavalry recoiled in shock. Jin forces pressed the attack and the Khitan broke and fled—but the ice on the Sha was thin, and many drowned.
entries.literal: The barbarian cavalry were startled and slightly retreated; Jin troops pressed them and the barbarians then scattered in flight; but the Sha River ice was thin and the barbarians all sank and drowned.

entries.zh: 阿保機退保望都。
entries.en: Abaoji fell back to Wangdu.
entries.literal: Abaoji withdrew to hold Wangdu.

entries.zh: 會天大雪，契丹人馬饑寒，多死，阿保機顧盧文進以手指天曰：「天未使我至此。」
entries.en: Heavy snow fell; Khitan men and horses starved and froze, and many died. Abaoji turned to Lu Wenjin, pointed at the sky, and said, "Heaven has not yet willed that I come here."
entries.literal: It happened that heaven sent great snow; Khitan men and horses were hungry and cold and many died; Abaoji turned to Lu Wenjin, pointing with his finger at heaven, saying: "Heaven has not yet brought me here.

entries.zh: 乃引兵去。
entries.en: He then withdrew his army.
entries.literal: Thereupon he led his troops away.

entries.zh: 莊宗躡其後，見其宿處，環稭在地，方隅整然，雖去而不亂，嘆曰：「虜法令嚴，蓋如此也！」
entries.en: Zhuangzong followed and inspected their camp: straw laid in a ring, corners neat and square—orderly even after they had gone. He sighed, "Their discipline is strict indeed!"
entries.literal: Zhuangzong followed on their heels, saw their camping place—straw arranged in a ring on the ground, corners square and orderly, though departed yet not disordered—and sighed: "Barbarian laws and orders are strict—probably just like this!"

entries.zh: 嗚呼，夷狄居處飲食，隨水草寒暑徙遷，有君長部號而無世族、文字記別，至於弦弓毒矢，強弱相並，國地大小，興滅不常，是皆烏足以考述哉！
entries.en: Alas—the barbarian peoples shift their camps with the seasons, grazing and drinking wherever grass and water lead them. They have chieftains and tribal names, but no hereditary clans or written records by which to distinguish lineages. Bent bows and poisoned arrows decide who annexes whom; realms wax and wane without pattern. None of this is fit matter for full historical treatment.
entries.literal: Alas, the barbarian peoples in their dwellings and diet follow grass and water, moving with cold and heat; they have chieftains and tribal names but no hereditary clans or written records for distinction; as for bent bows and poisoned arrows, the strong and weak annex one another, states and territories large and small, rise and fall without constancy—all these are utterly insufficient grounds for historical narration!

entries.zh: 惟其服叛去來，能為中國利害者，此不可以不知也。
entries.en: What we cannot afford to ignore is when they submit or rebel, come or go, and thereby help or harm the Central States.
entries.literal: Only their submission, rebellion, departure, and coming—those who can benefit or harm China—this one must not fail to know.

entries.zh: 自古夷狄之於中國，有道未必服，無道未必不來，蓋自因其衰盛。
entries.en: From antiquity, barbarian peoples have not submitted simply because the Central States upheld the Way, nor stayed away simply because they did not. Their conduct has always tracked our strength or weakness.
entries.literal: From antiquity the barbarian peoples toward China: when there is the Way they do not necessarily submit; when there is no Way they do not necessarily stay away—this is generally according to China's decline or flourishing.

entries.zh: 雖嘗置之治外，而羈縻制馭恩威之際，不可失也。
